title: Why does AI forget details in long chats?
style: midnight blue dark, teal accent, calm curious storytelling

lines: Jake has been chatting with his AI for *hours*.
Then it asks for his *name* again.

bg.intent: a long chat, then a forgotten name
subject: jake_neutral
chat

lines: Why does that happen?
The short answer: its working *memory* has a *limit*.
Every AI chat runs inside something called a *context window*.

bg.intent: name of the thing: the context window
subject: jake_think
notepad

lines: Picture it as a *notepad* with a fixed amount of space.
Everything you type goes onto that notepad.

bg.intent: your messages pile onto the notepad
subject: jake_happy
chat

lines: Every reply the AI writes goes on the *same* notepad.

bg.intent: its replies share the same space
subject: jake_think
chat

lines: So the longer you talk, the *fuller* it gets.

bg.intent: the notepad fills as the chat grows
subject: jake_worried
notepad

lines: The space is not counted in words.
It is counted in *tokens*.
A token is a small chunk of text, a bit less than one *word* on average.
Short, common words are usually one token.
Long words get *split* into pieces.

bg.intent: long words are split into tokens
subject: tokens

lines: Windows range from about *one hundred thousand* to a *million* tokens.
When the notepad is full, something has to *go*.
Some tools drop the oldest messages.
Others *summarize* them to save room.
That is one reason a chat can seem to forget *early* details.
But here is the *catch*.
Jake's chat was not even *full*.

bg.intent: the twist: it forgot before the notepad was full
subject: jake_surprised
notepad

lines: Researchers have a name for this: *context rot*.
As the text grows, an AI's accuracy and recall slowly *drop*.
Even *simple* tasks got less reliable as the input grew.
Tests on many popular models showed the same *trend*.

bg.intent: the same trend across many models
subject: tokens
jake_neutral

lines: A second study found a *position* effect.
Models had to find one fact hidden inside a long *text*.

bg.intent: a fact hidden in long text
subject: pages
note

lines: They did best when the fact sat at the *start* or the *end*.

bg.intent: best at the start or end
subject: strip
jake_happy

lines: In the *middle*, performance dropped sharply.
That held even for models *built* for long text.
So here is what happened to Jake's AI.
The notepad can *fill* up.

bg.intent: full answer part one: the notepad fills
subject: jake_blank
notepad

lines: And the *middle* of a long chat gets fuzzy.

bg.intent: full answer part two: the middle is fuzzy
subject: note
strip
jake_worried

lines: Does a bigger window fix it?
Not by *itself*.
What you put in the window matters as much as how *much* fits.
So repeat the *important* details near the end of your message.

bg.intent: tip one: repeat key details near the end
subject: jake_happy
note

lines: Or open a fresh chat with a short *summary*.

bg.intent: tip two: fresh chat with a summary
subject: jake_happy
chat

facts.claim: A context window is the text a model can consider at once, its working memory
The window holds your input, instructions and the model's own replies, so a long chat fills it
Space is counted in tokens; a token is a chunk of text, a bit less than one word on average; short common words are usually one token and long words are split
When the limit is exceeded, content must be truncated or summarized, so earlier parts of a long conversation can drop out
Context window sizes range from about 100 thousand tokens to a million or more depending on the model
As input length grows, accuracy and recall degrade (context rot), even on simple tasks, across many models
Models perform best when relevant information is at the start or end of a long input and much worse in the middle, even models built for long contexts
A larger context window does not automatically give better results; what is in the context matters as much as the space

post.pinned_comment: Jake is a fictional character and his story is an illustration. The facts come from AI documentation and research: a context window limits how much text a model can use at once, accuracy can drop as input grows (context rot), and models use information in the middle of long inputs less reliably than the start or end. The two tips at the end are practical suggestions based on these findings, not guarantees. Tomorrow: how does AI learn from its users?
